notes: Came to App State directly from the presidency of the University of South Florida (1988-1993), making him an external hire. His decade in Boone included major capital expansion and the founding of the Turchin Center for the Visual Arts. He died in 2025.

priorInstitution: Appalachian State University (same institution; he was App State's chief academic officer for 24 years)
notes: Officially titled Acting Chancellor for the 2003-04 academic year. He delayed his own retirement in June 2003 to hold the office while the UNC System searched for Borkowski's successor, then retired in 2004 after nearly 40 years at App State. He died May 15, 2026, at age 88.

priorTitle: Interim Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor
priorInstitution: Appalachian State University (same institution; he had been dean of its Walker College of Business until 2003)
notes: A fully internal appointment: he joined the App State accounting faculty in 1983 and was the Walker College of Business's fifth dean before moving into the provost's office. As chancellor he created the College of Health Sciences and moved athletics to the Sun Belt Conference and FBS. He died unexpectedly October 6, 2023, at age 75.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: External hire from Illinois State, where she had been provost since 2008. She was App State's first female chancellor, installed April 2015, and oversaw record enrollment growth past 21,000, roughly $550 million in capital investment, and the launch of the App State Hickory campus. She stepped down effective April 19, 2024, citing significant health challenges; her subsequent role is not publicly documented.

Named interim chancellor by UNC System President Peter Hans on April 19, 2024, the day Everts stepped down. She led the university through Hurricane Helene recovery while interim, which was widely credited in her subsequent permanent selection.

Elected by the UNC System Board of Governors on February 27, 2025 after a national search that drew more than 40 applicants, and took office March 1, 2025; formally installed October 3, 2025. She has spent her entire administrative career at App State, joining the finance faculty in 2003 and rising through assistant dean, dean of the Walker College of Business (2016-2020) and provost (2021-2024). No chancellor search is active.

Recruited by trustee and state senator Charles E. Bush, who was touring Southern agricultural schools for the new First District Agricultural School's board; Kays began June 1, 1910 and welcomed the first 189 students on October 3, 1910. His title evolved from principal to president as the school grew into a four-year college; he resigned in January 1943 after nearly 33 years, having led the institution through two world wars, the Depression and the 1931 fire that destroyed the main building.

A 1925 Aggie alumnus who succeeded V. C. Kays as the institution's second president in January 1943 and resigned in June 1945. His next role is not immediate: University of Arkansas at Monticello's official history records him as being named president of Arkansas A&M College in 1949, four years after he left Jonesboro. What he did between 1945 and 1949, and what he did immediately before 1943, could not be verified.

Second, interim stint. After Horace Thompson resigned in June 1945, Kays, who had stayed on campus as president emeritus and business manager, resumed the chief executive role for roughly a year until W. J. Edens arrived in April 1946. A wholly internal appointment. Kays died in 1966; the historic V. C. Kays House is an A-State heritage site.

Appointed Arkansas State's third president in April 1946, ending Kays's interim service. Edens resigned on March 21, 1951, after which Dean J. Walter Turner served as acting president. Neither his prior position nor his subsequent career could be verified from official or archival sources; the university's own history refers to him only as 'W. J. Edens.'

Internal caretaker appointment. The sitting dean of the college was named acting president on March 21, 1951, the day President Edens resigned, and served until the trustees named Carl R. Reng president on April 3, 1951, a vacancy filled in less than a month. What he did after the acting stint is not documented in the university's published history.

priorTitle: Head of the school administration division of the Graduate School
notes: External hire from the University of Arkansas, named fourth president on April 3, 1951, less than a month after Edens resigned. Over 24 years enrollment grew from 863 students and 81 faculty to more than 7,300 students and 342 faculty, and he led the successful campaign for university status in 1967, making Arkansas State the state's second university. Retired in 1975; the Reng Student Union is named for him. Died 1988.

External hire; a former Razorback football and track athlete and Peace Corps official who had managed an international company's interests in Iran before becoming president of Hood College in Maryland in 1972. Took office at Arkansas State in August 1975 and was credited with recruiting minority students and faculty, reorganizing the agriculture department and founding the Center for Continuing Education. Left in 1978 to become chancellor of the University of Denver, where he served until 1984. Died 2020.

External hire from the University of Arkansas, where he had been assistant to the president and vice president for governmental relations and public affairs before returning as vice president. At Arkansas State he created Convocation of Scholars Week and an agricultural cooperative program with the University of Arkansas. Resigned in January 1980 to enter private business, becoming president and CEO of the Arkansas electric cooperatives; a former legislator, he later served as a special assistant to President Bill Clinton. Died 2005.

First of Smith's two interim presidencies. A 1952 alumnus and long-time internal administrator, he was named interim president when Carl Whillock resigned in January 1980 and served until Ray Thornton took office later that year, then returned to his senior administrative post. Encyclopedia of Arkansas lists vice president for administration, dean of the Graduate School and senior vice president among his pre-presidential titles but does not date each transition, so his exact title at each moment is not fully documented.

priorInstitution: Joint Educational Consortium (Ouachita Baptist University and Henderson State University)
notes: Seventh president and an external hire. A former Arkansas attorney general and three-term U.S. Representative, he lost a 1978 Senate bid and returned to Arkansas in 1979 as executive director of the Joint Educational Consortium, the post he held immediately before Arkansas State. At ASU he raised the faculty's role in governance, reinstituted an interdisciplinary Honors Program and built an international training program for Saudi customs officers. In 1984 he was offered the University of Arkansas presidency without a formal search after the incumbent resigned unexpectedly; he later returned to Congress and served on the Arkansas Supreme Court. Died 2016.

Internal promotion, not an external hire: a 1952 ASC graduate who joined the faculty in 1958 and rose through executive assistant to President Reng, vice president for administration, dean of the Graduate School and senior vice president before being named the eighth president effective February 15, 1984, after Thornton left for the University of Arkansas. Enrollment grew from 8,319 in fall 1984 to 10,416 in fall 1991; he established the first doctoral program, opened the Convocation Center, expanded Dean B. Ellis Library and moved athletics to Division I. Announced retirement in August 1991 and was named president emeritus June 30, 1992. Died September 23, 2018.

Ninth president, hired in 1992 when Eugene Smith retired; implemented leadership and quality-assurance programs. His administration lasted only two years and he departed in spring 1994, triggering an unusually chaotic succession. Biographical directories report he came to Jonesboro from a provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs role at the University of New Orleans (1989-1992), after deanships at Texas Christian University, but this could not be confirmed against any official university, archival or news source, so the prior-role fields are left blank. His subsequent career is likewise unverified.

Internal appointment. The sitting vice president for academic affairs stepped up as interim president on Mangieri's departure in spring 1994 but died suddenly several months into the term, the first of two sudden deaths of long-time ASU administrators in the same year.

Internal appointment. Succeeded Hoskins as interim president in summer 1994 and died that fall, the second sudden death of a popular long-time university administrator within months. An Arkansas State student affairs award is named in his memory; he had also served as president of the Arkansas Student Affairs Association.

Third stint leading the campus and second interim presidency. Two years after retiring, the board called Smith back out of retirement to steady the university following the deaths of Hoskins and Richmond, and he ran the institution through the 1994-95 academic year while leading the nationwide search that produced Les Wyatt. Returned to retirement in summer 1995.

Tenth president, effective July 1, 1995, recruited from the University of Mississippi after the extensive national search run by interim president Eugene Smith; he had earlier held posts at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock from 1977 to 1988. Ushered in a new era of campus building expansion and served as both president of the emerging system and chief executive of the Jonesboro campus until the first Jonesboro chancellor was installed in fall 2006, when he moved to the system presidency full time. Resigned as system president in 2010 and was named president emeritus of the ASU System.

First chancellor of the Jonesboro campus and an external hire, appointed in the fall 2006 administrative reorganization that formally created the ASU System office and left Les Wyatt as system president. A lawyer by training (Alabama JD, Harvard LLM), he had been general counsel of the University of Alabama System, president of the University of North Alabama from 1990 to 2004, then chancellor of the North Dakota University System. Enrollment rose 23%, fundraising and research funding set records, and he created the Chancellor's Circle and the Beck Center for Veterans. In 2010 the trustees asked him to serve as interim system president; he retired in 2011 once Charles Welch was appointed and returned to Florence, Alabama. Died October 27, 2022.

priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Research and Provost
notes: Internal elevation: the sitting provost, who had come to A-State in 2007, was made interim chancellor in 2010 when Robert Potts moved to the interim system presidency, and led the campus for about two years. Known for a renewed push on international programs that sharply grew international enrollment and for launching online degree programs. Returned to full-time tenured faculty status in 2012 when Tim Hudson arrived, and was named chancellor of Louisiana State University of Alexandria in January 2014. An Army veteran with two doctorates, he died suddenly on January 30, 2022.

Second chancellor of the Jonesboro campus and an external hire: named March 2, 2012 and took office May 1, 2012, coming from a vice chancellor role at the Texas Tech University System that he had held since 2011, after serving as president of the University of Houston-Victoria (2004-2010) and provost at the University of Southern Mississippi. Resigned abruptly on August 3, 2016, effective immediately, after internal audits into nepotism and conflicts of interest in the study-abroad program his wife had overseen as part-time director. His subsequent role is not documented.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Research
notes: Internal stopgap. ASU System President Charles L. Welch named the sitting provost acting chancellor on August 3, 2016, the day Tim Hudson resigned, and she ran the campus for roughly a month until Doug Whitlock's interim appointment took effect in September 2016, after which she resumed the provost role. A 1979 A-State graduate who joined the biological sciences faculty in 1993 and had been dean of University College and associate dean of Arts and Sciences.

Brought out of retirement as a caretaker by ASU System President Charles L. Welch, starting September 12, 2016 on a prorated $305,000 salary through June 30, 2017, and expressly barred from candidacy for the permanent chancellorship so that a clean national search could begin in spring 2017. Then 73, he had spent 45 years at Eastern Kentucky University, including an interim presidency that became permanent, retiring as president in 2013.

priorTitle: Dean, College of Arts and Sciences
notes: Third chancellor and an external hire, announced May 17, 2017 and effective July 1, 2017, succeeding interim chancellor Doug Whitlock after a national search that drew 53 viable applications and brought three finalists to campus; the search advisory committee recommended him unanimously. He had been dean of the University of Oklahoma's College of Arts and Sciences since 2013. Announced on March 31, 2022 that he would resign effective June 30, 2022 to become president of Texas State University, where he started July 1, 2022.

priorTitle: Dean, J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences
notes: Fourth chancellor and an external hire from the University of Arkansas, where he had been Fulbright College dean since 2014; selected July 11, 2022 at a $450,000 salary and first day in office August 15, 2022. Because Damphousse left June 30 and Shields did not start until mid-August, the campus went roughly six weeks in summer 2022 with no publicly named interim chancellor. Enrollment grew nearly 30% under Shields and he launched the College of Veterinary Medicine, the Center for Advanced Materials and Steel Manufacturing and the CREST Center workforce program. On May 26, 2026 the ASU System Board of Trustees unanimously selected him as the system's fourth president, effective July 1, 2026, succeeding Brendan Kelly, who left in December 2025 to lead Eastern Michigan University; Robin Myers served as interim system president until Shields took over.

Internal appointment, not an external hire: interim system president Robin Myers recommended the sitting provost and executive vice chancellor, and the ASU System Board of Trustees voted unanimously on May 26, 2026 to name him interim chancellor effective July 1, 2026, the same day Shields became system president. He is the first African American to serve as either provost or chancellor at Arkansas State. A historian and native Arkansan with a Ph.D. from the University of Mississippi, he joined A-State as provost on July 1, 2023 from the University of Arkansas, where he had spent nearly 20 years and was associate dean of humanities in Fulbright College; as provost he took Arkansas's first and only College of Veterinary Medicine from concept to a first class in fall 2026 and oversaw growth past 17,000 students. As of July 24, 2026 neither A-State nor the ASU System had publicly announced a chancellor search committee, search firm or timeline for the Jonesboro campus; William McLean is serving as interim provost.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same institution, internal continuation; he had led ASU since July 1, 1995, before the 2006 system reorganization)
notes: First president of the ASU System. Formally titled James Leslie Wyatt, he became ASU president on July 1, 1995 and in October 2006 the Board of Trustees created a separate system office, with Wyatt remaining as system president and Robert L. Potts named the first chancellor of the Jonesboro campus. He announced his resignation at the May 2010 quarterly board meeting, effective June 30, 2010, and was unanimously designated President Emeritus.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal appointment)
notes: Asked by the Board of Trustees to serve as interim system president from July 1, 2010 while a permanent successor to Les Wyatt was recruited; Dan Howard became interim Jonesboro chancellor on his recommendation. Potts had been president of the University of North Alabama (1990-2004), general counsel of the University of Alabama System, and chancellor of the North Dakota University System before becoming ASU-Jonesboro's first chancellor in fall 2006. He retired to Florence, Alabama in 2011 and died October 28, 2022.

priorInstitution: Henderson State University, Arkadelphia, Arkansas (a separate Arkansas public university, not in the ASU System)
notes: Second president of the ASU System, known publicly as Chuck Welch. Named by the Board of Trustees in November 2010 and formally beginning in April 2011, he became the longest-tenured higher education president or chancellor in Arkansas over nearly 13 years. Earlier ASU System and Arkansas roles included chancellor of UA Community College at Hope-Texarkana and vice chancellor for academic affairs at ASU-Beebe. He resigned in November 2023, was designated President Emeritus in December 2023, and became AASCU's seventh president and CEO on January 15, 2024; the ASU System's own timeline lists his tenure as 2011-2023.

priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus (retired Chancellor of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home)
priorInstitution: Arkansas State University-Mountain Home (same system, internal appointment)
notes: First of two interim presidencies. Announced December 8, 2023 and effective January 15, 2024, he was chosen for his familiarity with the system and its leadership; the board stated he would not be a candidate for the permanent job. He had retired in July 2023 after 11 years as chancellor of ASU-Mountain Home and was designated Chancellor Emeritus on July 18, 2023. He served until Brendan Kelly took office on September 23, 2024.

priorInstitution: University of West Georgia, Carrollton, Georgia
notes: Third president of the ASU System, selected by the Board of Trustees on June 5, 2024 and beginning September 23, 2024. He came from the University of West Georgia presidency, which he had held since 2020, after earlier service as chancellor of USC Upstate, interim president of the University of South Carolina, and vice president for advancement at the University of West Florida. He announced his departure on December 10, 2025 to become president of his alma mater Eastern Michigan University, starting there April 1, 2026.

priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home and ASU System consultant; previously interim ASU System president in 2024
priorInstitution: Arkansas State University System (same system, internal appointment)
notes: Second interim presidency. The Board of Trustees named him interim system president on December 12, 2025, effective immediately, on contract terms consistent with his previous interim service and without scheduling a permanent search at that meeting. He served until Todd Shields took office July 1, 2026, and recommended A-State provost Calvin White Jr. as interim Jonesboro chancellor.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal promotion; he was chancellor from August 15, 2022 to June 30, 2026)
notes: Fourth president of the ASU System, appointed by unanimous vote of the Board of Trustees at a special called meeting on May 26, 2026, effective July 1, 2026, succeeding Brendan Kelly (with Robin Myers serving as interim in between). A political scientist with a Ph.D. from the University of Kentucky, he was dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at the University of Arkansas from 2014 before being named A-State's chancellor on July 11, 2022, where he oversaw an enrollment increase of nearly 30 percent as the fourth appointed chancellor and 14th person to lead the Jonesboro campus.

priorInstitution: Medical College of Georgia (same institution; he joined the MCG faculty in 1978 as chief of gastroenterology)
notes: Internal promotion; president of the Medical College of Georgia from July 1, 1988 until his retirement February 1, 2001, the longest presidency of the modern era. The institution he led is the direct predecessor of Augusta University. A gastroenterologist, he received the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy's Rudolf Schindler Award in 1993.

priorTitle: Senior Vice President for Medical Affairs and Chief Medical Officer, MCG Health Inc.
notes: Internal promotion, named by the Georgia Board of Regents effective June 1, 2001. A rheumatologist known for Lyme disease research, he left in 2009 to become chancellor of UAMS, where he served until retiring in 2017.

An otolaryngologist and former medical school dean, named interim president of the Medical College of Georgia by the University System of Georgia; he joined MCG October 1, 2009 and held the office until Azziz arrived in 2010. His immediately preceding position could not be verified from an official source.

priorTitle: Professor and Chair, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, and Director, Center for Androgen-Related Research and Discovery
notes: External hire. He presided over the institution's rebranding to Georgia Health Sciences University (2011) and the contentious consolidation with Augusta State University into Georgia Regents University (2013), and was founding CEO of the Georgia Regents Health System. He announced on January 15, 2015 that he would step down effective June 30, 2015.

External hire from within the same state system, taking office July 20, 2015; the institution was renamed Augusta University on December 1, 2015, months into his term. He holds undergraduate and graduate degrees from Augusta's legacy institutions. Under him enrollment grew about 25 percent, NIH funding rose 37 percent, and the School of Computer and Cyber Sciences was created. He retired June 30, 2024.

priorTitle: Executive Vice President for Administration and Chief of Staff to the President
priorInstitution: Augusta University (same institution; he had held that role since July 2015)
notes: A fully internal appointment named by the Georgia Board of Regents on June 14, 2024 and effective July 1, 2024. An Augusta native and first-generation college graduate, he spent 2001-2015 at Georgia Southern University rising to vice president for external affairs before joining Augusta as Keel's chief of staff. No presidential search is active; the open searches at Augusta are for executive cabinet positions.

Ball State's 11th president and the person in office at the 1996 scope boundary; external hire who came from the presidency of Indiana University of Pennsylvania (1979-1984). His 16-year tenure is among the longest in Ball State history and was honored in the Congressional Record on his 2000 retirement.

Ball State's 12th president. An urban historian, he served as provost and vice president for academic affairs at the University of North Texas from 1990 to 1998, but the position he held immediately before the 2000 Ball State appointment could not be verified from an official source, so it is left blank. He resigned effective January 1, 2004.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Ball State's 13th president, serving roughly seven months as interim after Brownell's resignation. A journalism professor by background, she left the interim role to become president of the University of Indianapolis, where she served until retiring in 2011.

Ball State's 14th president and its first woman to hold the office permanently; external hire from UMass Boston, where she had been chancellor since 2001 (and before that provost at Old Dominion University). She announced in October 2013 that she would retire June 30, 2014 after a decade marked by large-scale campus construction and the geothermal energy conversion.

Ball State's 15th president, appointed May 2014 and beginning duties August 1, 2014 as an external hire from the University of Maine presidency. A toxicologist, he resigned abruptly on January 25, 2016 after requesting a two-month sabbatical; the board of trustees gave no reason, and his next position is not publicly documented.

priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Ball State's 16th president, serving as acting president from January 2016 until Mearns took office in 2017. He had also briefly filled the gap between Gora's June 2014 retirement and Ferguson's August 2014 arrival. His post-acting-presidency role is not documented in an official source.

Ball State's 17th president, named January 2017 and taking office in May 2017 as an external hire from Northern Kentucky University, where he had been president since 2012. A former federal prosecutor and law dean at Cleveland State, he oversaw Ball State's 2018 assumption of governance of Muncie Community Schools. Trustees voted May 1, 2026 to extend his contract through June 30, 2029, so no presidential search is active.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Boise State's fifth president and the person in office at the 1996 scope boundary; external hire from Virginia Commonwealth University, where he was provost 1985-1993. Under him the operating budget grew from $91.8 million to $222.9 million. After South Dakota Mines (2003-2008) he served interim deanships at Texas Tech and Armstrong State.

Boise State's sixth president, an external hire and former lieutenant governor of Illinois who had been president of Eastern Kentucky University (1998-2002) before leading the Midwestern Higher Education Compact. His 15-year tenure produced Boise State's 2016 Carnegie doctoral research university designation and major research growth. He announced his retirement in November 2017, effective June 2018.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Named interim president by the Idaho State Board of Education for the year between Kustra's retirement and Tromp's arrival. He joined the Boise State chemistry department in 1990 and was provost from 2010 to 2018, a period in which the university built Idaho's largest graduate school.

priorTitle: Campus Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor
notes: Boise State's seventh president and its first woman president, an external hire who took office July 1, 2019 and was invested October 3, 2019. A Victorian literature scholar and first-generation college graduate, her tenure was politically turbulent, with sustained legislative scrutiny of diversity programming. She announced her departure March 20, 2025 to become the 28th president of the University of Vermont, starting there July 1, 2025.

priorTitle: Vice President for Student Affairs and Enrollment Management
notes: Appointed interim president by the Idaho State Board of Education and began May 10, 2025, after spring commencement. He had served at Boise State from 2010 to 2019 and returned as vice president in February 2023. In April 2026 he was named sole finalist and then the 20th president of the University of Montana, starting there July 1, 2026.

priorTitle: Vice President for Research and Economic Development
notes: Named acting president in May 2026 to cover the short gap between Shinn's departure for Montana and Hahn's July 1, 2026 start; her tenure lasted only weeks. She reported to the State Board in June 2026 that Boise State had met the thresholds for Carnegie R1 research designation.

priorTitle: Craig M. Berge Dean of the College of Engineering
notes: Boise State's eighth president, an external hire appointed unanimously by the Idaho State Board of Education on July 1, 2026 after a search conducted under a 2026 Idaho law that closed the process and required naming only a single finalist. A thermal sciences and energy researcher with more than 130 peer-reviewed papers and 12 U.S. patents, he spent 21 years at the University of Florida before Arizona. His appointment was effective July 1, 2026, with on-campus duties required by August 10, 2026, so the 14-month presidential search is now closed.

BGSU's ninth president and first African American president; the sitting leader in 1996, included with his true 1995 start year to anchor the chain. Announced in May 2008 that he was leaving to lead Howard University, where he began August 1, 2008. BGSU trustees granted him the title President Emeritus in May 2017.

priorTitle: President Emerita (retired 2006 after serving as President 1991-2006)
notes: Came out of retirement as interim president in July 2008 and was named BGSU's tenth president on January 6, 2009, so the entry is recorded as a full presidency rather than interim. She is president emerita of both Kent State and BGSU, an unusual double.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: BGSU's eleventh president, taking office July 1, 2011. She announced at the December 2017 board meeting that she would step down on December 31, 2017, a year early on a contract running through 2019, and trustees named her President Emeritus at the same meeting.

priorTitle: Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: Bowling Green State University (internal; provost since 2012, before that dean of the Schmidthorst College of Business 2006-2012)
notes: Named interim president effective January 1, 2018 and appointed BGSU's twelfth president on February 23, 2018; the first BGSU alumnus to lead the university. Still sitting as of July 2026 with no active presidential search identified.

Fourth president; the sitting leader in 1996, included with his true 1991 start year to anchor the chain. Came from CSUN, where he was VP for Academic Affairs 1985-1991. Known for diversity and educational-equity work, founding the cultural centers and iPoly High School.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Fifth president, appointed by the CSU Board of Trustees in 2003 after serving as provost at Fresno State (1999-2003). Announced his retirement January 30, 2014, effective at the end of December 2014; his tenure secured a $42 million Kellogg Foundation gift, then the largest cash gift in CSU history. No interim served between him and Coley, who began January 1, 2015.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Sixth president and the first woman and first African American to lead Cal Poly Pomona; appointed September 2014 and took office January 1, 2015 after serving as CSU Bakersfield's provost 2005-2014. Announced February 4, 2025 that she would retire at the end of July 2025. Her tenure drew a nonbinding Academic Senate no-confidence resolution (25-3) on December 6, 2023 over shared-governance concerns.

priorTitle: Interim Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs (last active post before her 2022 retirement)
priorInstitution: California State Polytechnic University, Pomona (internal; she came out of retirement from this same campus)
notes: Seventh president, serving in an interim capacity from July 28, 2025 to June 30, 2026. A 32-year Cal Poly Pomona veteran: joined the music faculty in 1990, chaired the Music Department, then served as dean of the College of Letters, Arts and Social Sciences and interim provost before retiring in 2022. She is also founder and artistic director of VOX Femina Los Angeles.

Eighth president and the first Latina to lead Cal Poly Pomona; named by the CSU Board of Trustees in March 2026 following a national search launched after Coley's retirement, and took office July 1, 2026, so she is the sitting president as of July 2026 and there is no active presidential search. She had been the fourth president of CSU Monterey Bay since 2022; earlier provost at Pace University and 21 years at CUNY Hunter College. A neurobiologist by training (PhD, Rutgers).

Took office July 29, 1991 after leading Indiana University of Pennsylvania (president 1985-91). The sitting leader in 1996, included with his true 1991 start year. Longest-serving modern Fresno State president at 22 years; announced retirement in August 2012 and was honored at a June 12, 2013 farewell reception. The John D. Welty Center for Educational Policy and Leadership is named for him.

priorTitle: Vice Chancellor for Student Academic Affairs and Professor of Family and Community Medicine
notes: Named by the CSU Board of Trustees in May 2013 and took office August 1, 2013 as Fresno State's eighth president; first Mexican American and first California native to lead the campus. Left after trustees selected him as system chancellor, a post he began January 4, 2021; he resigned the chancellorship in February 2022 amid criticism of his handling of a sexual harassment complaint during his Fresno State presidency. Died of cancer August 25, 2025 at age 58.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: California State University, Fresno (internal; provost since July 2019, earlier dean of the College of Arts and Humanities)
notes: Named interim president by Chancellor Timothy P. White in October 2020 and began January 4, 2021, the same day Castro started as CSU chancellor. Served roughly four and a half months in the interim role before the trustees made the appointment permanent.

priorInstitution: California State University, Fresno (internal; before the interim role, Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs at Fresno State)
notes: Appointed Fresno State's ninth president by the CSU Board of Trustees on May 19, 2021, moving up from the interim role. A Fresno State insider: faculty member in Spanish and Portuguese for nearly 15 years, then dean and provost; he immigrated from Mexico at age 10. His tenure has drawn friction, including a September 2024 union petition calling for his resignation and, in 2026, his removal of five longtime Fresno State Foundation board members after a critical Chancellor's Office review. No presidential search is under way; he remains the sitting president as of July 2026.

priorTitle: Vice President for Academic Affairs and Professor of Mathematics
notes: Became CSUF's fourth president in August 1990; the sitting leader in 1996, included with his true 1990 start year. Longest-serving president in campus history, with enrollment growing from about 25,600 to 36,000. Announced retirement at the fall 2011 convocation and stepped down as interim president Willie Hagan took office January 9, 2012. University Hall was renamed Milton A. Gordon Hall in his honor in 2019.

priorTitle: Vice President for Administration and Chief Financial Officer
notes: A 16-year CSUF administrator, Hagan was named interim president effective January 9, 2012 and served until June 10, 2012. In an unusual swap, he became interim president of CSU Dominguez Hills effective June 11, 2012, the same day Dominguez Hills president Mildred Garcia started at Fullerton; he was later made CSUDH's permanent president and retired in 2018.

Appointed by the CSU Board of Trustees on January 25, 2012; her first day at CSUF was June 11, 2012, making her the campus's fifth trustee-appointed president and the first Latina president in the CSU system. Named AASCU president in November 2017 and departed at the end of 2017 (Framroze Virjee took office January 1, 2018). She led AASCU 2018-2023 and then became the 11th Chancellor of the California State University effective October 1, 2023.

priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor, General Counsel and Secretary to the Board of Trustees
notes: Assumed the CSUF presidency January 1, 2018 under a term/interim appointment made by Chancellor Timothy P. White after Mildred Garcia left for AASCU. He served as CSU's executive vice chancellor and general counsel from January 2014 through December 2017, and before that was a partner for nearly 30 years at the law firm O'Melveny & Myers.

priorInstitution: California State University, Fullerton (internal; already serving as CSUF's term-appointed president)
notes: The CSU Board of Trustees named him permanent president on March 20, 2019 following a national search, making him the campus's sixth trustee-appointed president. He announced on January 23, 2023 that he would retire effective July 31, 2023 at age 62, and was named president emeritus. AGB named him its next president and CEO, a role he began August 19, 2024.

priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic and Student Affairs
notes: Appointed interim president by CSU Interim Chancellor Jolene Koester in April 2023, effective August 1, 2023, to serve until the trustees named a permanent president. She led the campus through the 2023-24 year and the national presidential search, and stepped aside when Ronald S. Rochon took office July 22, 2024. Her post-CSUF role could not be verified from official or press sources.

Appointed by the CSU Board of Trustees on May 22, 2024 and took office July 22, 2024 as CSUF's 10th president, succeeding interim president Sylvia Alva. He had been president of the University of Southern Indiana since 2018; a first-generation college graduate from Chicago's South Side with a doctorate in educational policy studies from Illinois. Still sitting as of July 2026; the 2024 search that produced him has concluded, so no active presidential search.

Sixth president; the sitting leader in 1996, included with his true June 1994 start year. Came from UNLV, where he was president 1984-1994. Branded the campus 'The Beach' and coined 'Go Beach!' Left in January 2006 to lead Sierra Nevada College, then retired; died in 2025 at age 89.

Seventh president, taking office January 2006 after serving as president of Murray State University (2001-2005). Left CSULB in June 2013 to become president of the LSU System (2013-2019), and later president of Oregon State University (2019-2021).

priorTitle: Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: California State University, Long Beach (internal; earlier Dean of the College of the Arts)
notes: Named interim president effective July 1, 2013 by CSU Chancellor Timothy White after Alexander's departure for LSU; served through June 2014. He was CSULB's sitting provost before stepping up, and retired after the interim term.

priorTitle: Dean of the Gevirtz Graduate School of Education
notes: First woman to serve as CSULB president; took office July 2014 from her deanship at UCSB's Gevirtz School (where she had also been interim chancellor at UC Riverside 2012-2013). Retired effective June 30, 2025 after roughly 11 years.

priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor and General Counsel
priorInstitution: The California State University Chancellor's Office
notes: CSULB alumnus (class of 1982) named acting president effective August 25, 2025, bridging the gap after Conoley's retirement. Came from the CSU Chancellor's Office, where he was executive vice chancellor, general counsel, and secretary to the Board of Trustees. Served until Blanchard took office May 1, 2026.

Appointed by the CSU Board of Trustees on January 28, 2026; assumed office May 1, 2026 as the sitting president. Came directly from a five-year presidency at the University of Houston-Downtown, and earlier spent six years as CSU Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic and Student Affairs. The national search concluded in January 2026, so no active presidential search.

priorTitle: Vice Chancellor of Higher Education (and Acting Chancellor, 1977)
priorInstitution: New Jersey Department of Higher Education
notes: Sixth president and by far the longest-serving in campus history at 34 years; in office throughout 1996, so his true 1979 start is recorded here. Earlier he was associate vice chancellor for academic affairs at the University of Kansas. The campus dedicated James M. Rosser Hall in his honor in 2017.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Seventh president; external to the campus but internal to the CSU system, arriving from the Fresno provostship (and earlier the Stanislaus State provostship). Announced his retirement in August 2022, effective June 30, 2023.

priorTitle: President Emeritus (retired from the presidency in 2020)
notes: Appointed interim president by CSU Interim Chancellor Jolene Koester; served July 31, 2023 to January 7, 2024. A 40-year CSU veteran who led Cal State East Bay 2011-2020 and spent 30 years at San Francisco State before that.

priorInstitution: York College, City University of New York
notes: Ninth president and the first woman to lead Cal State LA; took office January 8, 2024. External hire from CUNY, though she had earlier been vice president for student affairs at Cal State Fullerton (2012-2019). No active presidential search found.

Longest-serving Sacramento State president (19 years); in office throughout 1996, so his true 1984 start is recorded. Came from the Dominguez Hills presidency (1976-1984), so a CSU-internal but campus-external move. Later wrote a history of the CSU system.

Led Sacramento State for 12 years after six years as president of CSU San Marcos; earlier spent 18 years at Fresno State as faculty member, department chair and provost. Another CSU-internal, campus-external move.

priorTitle: Special Advisor to the Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
notes: Eighth permanent president, appointed March 2015 and took office July 1, 2015. Immediately prior he advised the UT System after serving as president of the University of Texas-Pan American (2010-2014). Announced his retirement November 2, 2022; last day July 1, 2023.

priorTitle: Vice President for Student Affairs and Campus Diversity and Chief Diversity Officer
notes: Ninth permanent president, took office July 16, 2023. A Sacramento State alumnus (BA in Black History and Politics, MA in Higher Education Leadership) and a former foster child; at SDSU he was the first Black Distinguished Professor in that institution's history. No active presidential search found.

Eleventh president; a fully internal promotion after 20 years at CMU as business professor, assistant dean and then dean of the College of Business Administration (1979-92). Named interim president in 1992 and permanent president in 1994; retired July 31, 2000. In office throughout 1996.

Twelfth president. Began his higher education career as president of Mission College in California, then chancellor of Montana State University-Northern (1998-2000) before CMU. Left in 2009 to become the fifth president of Virginia Commonwealth University and VCU Health System.

priorTitle: Vice President for Government Relations and Public Affairs
notes: Thirteenth president and the first woman to lead CMU, serving on an interim basis after Rao's departure. Joined CMU in 2002 after a career in Michigan state government, where she was the first woman to direct three state departments. Died in 2023.

Fourteenth president, serving March 1, 2010 to July 31, 2018. Returned to CMU from the Alcorn State presidency, having previously been CMU's vice president for finance and administrative services, so an external appointment with prior campus ties.

Fifteenth president, appointed September 1, 2018. Had earlier been president of Eastern Oregon University before Murray State. Announced in January 2024 that he would step down effective December 31, 2024, citing personal and professional reasons; his successor took office November 1, 2024, so no interim was needed.

priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Sixteenth president, appointed unanimously by the Board of Trustees in September 2024 and took office November 1, 2024. A pharmacist by training with 26 years in higher education; formally invested in April 2025. No active presidential search found.

Fourth president and the first woman to lead Cleveland State, taking office April 20, 1993; in office throughout 1996. Oversaw the conversion to the semester system in 1998. Died September 29, 2021 at age 86 of injuries from a car crash in Needham, Massachusetts.

Fifth president. Served roughly one year as interim president beginning in 2001 before being appointed president and installed September 26, 2002; the official past-presidents list therefore dates his term 2002-2009. Previously president of Kent State University (1982-1991). Built enrollment standards, an honors program, and major new buildings including the Student Center and Recreation Center.

Sixth president, 2009-2018, per the university's official past-presidents list. His immediately preceding position and his post-presidency role could not be confirmed from official or press sources within this research pass and are deliberately left blank.

Seventh president. Departed April 26, 2022 after four years in what the Board of Trustees called a mutually agreed-upon separation over differences about the university's future direction; he was not fired and no single triggering event was cited. His package included roughly $928,000 and the option of a tenured professorship at the Cleveland-Marshall College of Law, though it is unconfirmed whether he took it. Prior position not verified.

priorTitle: Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Eighth president, appointed April 26, 2022 and promoted straight from the provostship with no interim designation and no national search. She had joined Cleveland State in fall 2021 from the University of Minnesota, where she was dean of the Humphrey School of Public Affairs. Was a finalist for the University of Minnesota presidency in February 2024 but was passed over and stated she has no intention of seeking another presidency. No active presidential search found.

priorTitle: Dean, College of Arts and Sciences
priorInstitution: North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University
notes: Eighth president, took office July 1, 1987 and served 16 years, the second-longest tenure in DSU history; his presidency spanned the 1993 elevation from Delaware State College to Delaware State University. Retired June 30, 2003 and died May 21, 2019 at age 81.

priorTitle: Fellow and Lecturer, Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, John F. Kennedy School of Government
notes: Ninth president, effective July 1, 2003; a Yale physics Ph.D. and former U.S. State Department diplomat who had been president of Queens College, CUNY (1995 to 2000) before his Harvard fellowship. Launched DSU's first doctoral programs but drew a 2005 no-confidence vote and low faculty-confidence survey; resigned August 30, 2008 to lead UDC, where he was later fired in 2012.

Acting president September 1, 2008 to January 9, 2010; a retired DuPont research chemist and longtime DSU board member who stepped aside from the board chairmanship to run the university during the search that produced Harry Williams. He resumed the chairmanship in 2010 and the campus administration building was named for him in 2015.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Internal promotion: sworn in as 10th president January 10, 2010 after 18 months as DSU provost; earlier held posts at the University of North Carolina General Administration, Appalachian State and North Carolina A&T. DSU rose sharply in HBCU rankings during his tenure; he left at the end of 2017 to lead the Thurgood Marshall College Fund and was named DSU president emeritus in 2021.

Served as acting president January 2 to June 30, 2018 after Williams departed, then was elected 11th president by unanimous board vote effective July 1, 2018; the first woman to chair the DSU board and the first woman to lead the university. A four-decade higher-education administrator, she announced her retirement effective December 31, 2019 and rejoined the DSU board in January 2020.

Internal promotion: became 12th president January 1, 2020 after joining DSU as provost in 2017 from Bank of America; earlier an executive VP at MBNA America and a speechwriter for then-Senator Joseph R. Biden Jr. Chaired the President's Board of Advisors on HBCUs from 2021 to January 2025 and was CEO of the 59th Presidential Inaugural Committee; oversaw the acquisition of Wesley College. Still sitting as of July 2026; no active presidential search found.

priorTitle: Director of Academic Affairs, corporate office
notes: Seventh president. Took office May 4, 1992 (initially as interim, made permanent by the Tennessee Board of Regents in 1993); ETSU's official list records his tenure as 1992 to 1996 without an interim designation. A veteran Tennessee higher-education and state-government figure who had been TBR chancellor 1975 to 1986. Retired December 31, 1996.

priorTitle: Vice President for Health Affairs and Dean, James H. Quillen College of Medicine
notes: Eighth president, an internal promotion: a board-certified vascular surgeon who came to ETSU in 1985 and rose from faculty to dean of the medical college to vice president for health affairs before the Tennessee Board of Regents named him president effective January 1, 1997. No interim separated him from Nicks. His 15-year tenure produced the Gatton College of Pharmacy, the Honors College and the Gray Fossil Site. He died March 5, 2026 at age 81.

priorInstitution: West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission
notes: Ninth president, an external hire who took office January 15, 2012 after five years leading West Virginia's statewide higher-education coordinating board. He led ETSU through the 2016 FOCUS Act transition to its own Board of Trustees in 2017, relaunched football, and oversaw the R2 Carnegie classification. The Board of Trustees approved a new five-year contract in November 2023; he remains in office as of July 2026 with no active presidential search.

priorInstitution: East Texas State University (this same institution before its 1996 renaming)
notes: Ninth president, in office January 1, 1987 to late 1997; a career internal who joined the campus in 1970 and rose through dean of admissions, graduate dean and chief academic officer. He led the drive that took East Texas State University into The Texas A&M University System on September 1, 1996, triggering the rename to Texas A&M University-Commerce. He died of cancer December 11, 2008 at age 73.

priorTitle: Dean of Graduate Studies (1983 to 1997), then Interim President in early 1998
notes: Tenth president; a pure internal promotion, a historian on the faculty since 1969 who was graduate dean 1983 to 1997, ran the university as interim in early 1998, and was named president and CEO in September 1998. He announced retirement in August 2007 effective July 31, 2008; the campus science building was named for him in 2013.

priorTitle: Provost, Vice President for Academic Affairs and Professor of English
notes: Eleventh president, taking office July 2008 after five years as chief academic officer at Texas A&M International University (a fellow A&M System member), so internal to the A&M System rather than fully external. He died unexpectedly April 29, 2016 at age 63 while still the sitting president; Inside Higher Ed subsequently reported the death was ruled a suicide.

Twelfth president. Named interim president effective June 1, 2016 after Dan Jones's death, moving directly from the TAMIU presidency; the A&M System Board of Regents named him sole finalist in October 2016 and he became permanent president November 10, 2016, so his term was only partly interim. He announced in January 2018 that he would step down effective August 31, 2018, and a search committee was formed in February 2018.

priorTitle: Vice President for Research and Economic Development
notes: Thirteenth president and CEO, named sole finalist in July 2018 and appointed by the A&M System Board of Regents August 16, 2018; a genuinely external hire from Boise State, with a Ph.D. in medicinal chemistry from Purdue. He remains in office as of July 2026 with no presidential search under way; the institution was renamed from Texas A&M University-Commerce to East Texas A&M University effective November 2024 during his tenure.
President in office during 1996; served 1989 to June 2000, an external hire from Kent State. After EMU he moved to East Carolina University, where he later became interim chancellor.

priorInstitution: University of Texas at San Antonio
notes: External hire; had been president of the University of Texas at San Antonio in the 1990s and was affiliated with AASCU immediately before EMU. His presidency ended in 2004 amid Board of Regents conflict.

Internal appointee. Named acting president at the August 2004 Board of Regents meeting for roughly two weeks, bridging Kirkpatrick's departure and interim President Willis's arrival, then became interim provost.

One-year interim appointment effective August 16, 2004 through July 31, 2005. Had been president of Lock Haven University (PA) for 22 years and was credited with restoring campus morale after Kirkpatrick's departure.

priorInstitution: State University of New York at Potsdam
notes: External hire from SUNY Potsdam. Fired by the Board of Regents July 15, 2007 over the university's handling and delayed disclosure of the December 2006 rape and murder of student Laura Dickinson (Clery Act violations). He later sued EMU and in 2012 took an administrative post at Ball State University.

priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Internal. Served as senior administrative official/acting head after Fallon's firing until Susan Martin was hired in 2008, then returned to the provostship and later to faculty.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
notes: EMU's 22nd president and its first female president, from the U-M Dearborn provostship. Announced her departure in March 2015 with a final day of July 7, 2015, took a sabbatical, then returned to EMU as a faculty member.

priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice President of Academic and Student Affairs
notes: Internal appointee; interim president from July 7, 2015. Departed to become president of Towson University (MD) effective January 2016. (She later moved to the University of Texas at Arlington in 2020, but the role immediately after EMU was the Towson presidency.)

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs (retired 2014)
notes: Came out of retirement for a third stint in the president's office, serving as interim president from December 2015 to June 2016 until James Smith arrived.

External hire from Northern State University (Aberdeen, SD); began July 1, 2016 and served roughly a decade. He stepped aside at the end of his contract; Kelly began April 1, 2026 ahead of Smith's June 30, 2026 contract conclusion.

24th president; a two-time EMU alumnus and Flint native. Elected by the Board of Regents December 10, 2025; joined March 1, 2026 as president-elect and began as president April 1, 2026 on a five-year contract. Earlier roles include president of the University of West Georgia and chancellor of USC Upstate. The presidential search that selected him has concluded.

priorTitle: Dean of the School of Liberal Arts
notes: Twelfth president of Hunter College, 1995 to 2000. Came from Purdue University, where he had been dean of the School of Liberal Arts for eight years and a faculty member since 1969. Left Hunter in 2000 to become the sixth president of Pace University, where he served until 2007.

priorTitle: Acting Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Interim president July 2000 to June 2001, an internal promotion from Hunter's acting provost/senior VP for academic affairs (he had joined Hunter as VP for Administration in 1996). After the interim presidency he moved to Queens College as interim provost in 2001, became provost in 2003 until retiring in 2009, and later served as interim president of Queens College in spring 2014.

priorTitle: Chair, New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
priorInstitution: New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
notes: Thirteenth president, June 2001 to June 2023, one of the longest tenures in Hunter's history at 22 years; came directly from chairing the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission (1994 to 2001). She led Hunter's transformation into a selective, highly ranked college and raised more than $500 million. Her December 2022 announcement that she would step down was widely reported as sudden. In January 2024 she became president and CEO of The New York Stem Cell Foundation.

priorTitle: Dean Emerita, Macaulay Honors College (former University Professor, CUNY Graduate Center)
priorInstitution: The City University of New York
notes: Interim president July 1, 2023 to August 2024, bridging Raab and Cantor. Dean emerita of CUNY's Macaulay Honors College, which she led 2006 to 2016, and previously a University Professor at the CUNY Graduate Center. After the interim term she continued as a professor of practice and special adviser to the president at Arizona State University and as a writer on higher education.

Fourteenth president, took office August 12, 2024. Came from a decade as chancellor of Rutgers University-Newark (2014 to June 2023); earlier she was chancellor and president of Syracuse University and chancellor of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. A social psychologist, she is the daughter of a Hunter College alumna. Still sitting as of July 2026; no active presidential search.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Vice President for Academic Affairs and Professor of Anthropology
notes: Tenth president and the first woman to lead City College; in office throughout 1996, so her true 1993 start is recorded. Left July 2, 1999 under pressure from CUNY trustees during the fight over remediation and admissions policy. Later became associate vice chancellor at UC Riverside.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Dean, Sophie Davis School of Biomedical Education
priorInstitution: The City College of New York (same campus)
notes: Served as interim president between Moses's forced departure in 1999 and Gregory Williams's arrival in 2001, charged with redirecting the campus after the CUNY remediation fight. A fully internal appointment.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Dean of the Michael E. Moritz College of Law and Carter C. Kissell Professor of Law
notes: Eleventh president, taking office August 2001. Enrollment grew roughly 60 percent to more than 16,000; he opened The Towers residence hall, completed the Spitzer School of Architecture, and led a first capital campaign raising over $310 million. Resigned effective November 1, 2009 to become the 27th president of the University of Cincinnati. Author of the memoir 'Life on the Color Line'; died August 12, 2025.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Distinguished Professor of Civil Engineering and Director, University Transportation Research Center
priorInstitution: The City College of New York (same campus)
notes: Served as interim president from October 15, 2009 to August 2, 2010, bridging Williams's departure and Coico's arrival. A fully internal appointment; a nationally known transportation scholar who later received CCNY's President's Medal.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Provost and Senior Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: Twelfth president and a CCNY alumna, published at Temple under the name Lisa Staiano-Coico. Resigned abruptly in October 2016 while she and an affiliated nonprofit foundation were under federal investigation over her personal expenses and the handling of research funds. Her post-resignation role could not be verified.

university: The City College of New York
priorTitle: Dean, Colin Powell School for Civic and Global Leadership
priorInstitution: The City College of New York (same campus)
notes: Named interim president effective November 2, 2016 by CUNY Chancellor James B. Milliken after Coico's resignation, then appointed permanent president by the CUNY Board of Trustees on December 4, 2017; the single entry covers the continuous tenure. A fully internal appointment: founding director (2002-13) and founding dean (2013-16) of the Colin Powell School and a professor of political science specializing in Southeast Asian social movements. No active presidential search found.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College, which the Little Rock Board of Education created in 1927 and operated as a school-district institution. Hall held the college presidency while serving as Little Rock School District superintendent (1909-1941); Hall High School is named for him.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Larson, a Swedish-born high school principal, urged the Little Rock Board of Education to found LRJC in 1927 and is regarded as its founder; he resigned the Central High School principalship to devote himself to the college and died in office in 1949. The UA Little Rock official list gives 1930-1949; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas photo caption dates his presidency from 1929 and the UA Little Rock history page says 1930-1950.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Published as Granville D. Davis by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, which notes he was a member of the first LRJC graduating class, making him an alumnus-president. His immediately prior and subsequent positions could not be verified from available sources.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: acting president of Little Rock Junior College, as published on the university's official list of past presidents and chancellors. He bridged the two years between Granville Davis and Carey V. Stabler; no verifiable record of his prior or subsequent positions was found.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President. Under Stabler, Little Rock Junior College became the independent, private, four-year Little Rock University in fall 1957, and course offerings grew from roughly 80 in 1956 to about 500 by 1967. He continued in office when the institution joined the University of Arkansas System in 1969, at which point his title changed from president to chancellor. His position immediately before 1956 could not be verified.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorInstitution: Little Rock University (the same institution, before its 1969 merger into the UA System)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. Same person as the preceding entry, listed separately by the university because the 1969 merger of Little Rock University into the University of Arkansas System converted the office from president to chancellor. He resigned in 1972; Stabler Hall is named for him. What he did after resigning could not be verified.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: acting chancellor. Fribourgh, a biologist, joined Little Rock Junior College in 1949 and spent 45 years at the institution through its Little Rock University and UALR eras, serving as chief academic officer from 1969 to 1984 and stepping up as acting chancellor after Stabler's resignation. Fribourgh Hall and the university's Fribourgh Award are named for him; he died March 6, 2014.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Ross accepted the UALR chancellorship in January 1973 as chancellor and professor of education and psychology, and is credited with establishing UALR's autonomy within the UA System, growing degree programs from 28 to 73 and enrollment from about 3,500 to 9,652. He left in summer 1982, was named president of Western Washington University in January 1983, and was killed in a plane crash in November 1987 along with two WWU vice presidents and the pilot. He was also a past president of ACPA.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: acting chancellor. Fribourgh's second stint as acting chancellor, bridging G. Robert Ross's summer 1982 departure and James H. Young's arrival later that year; the university lists both of his acting terms in a single line (1972-1973, 1982).

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. Young emphasized a traditional liberal arts direction, established campus-wide learning goals, and opened UALR's first residential dormitory. His position immediately before 1982 and his destination after leaving in 1992 could not be verified from available sources; the University of Arkansas holds biographical materials on him in its archives.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: interim chancellor. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas records that Anderson, then UALR's provost, served as interim chancellor in 1993 between James H. Young and Charles E. Hathaway; the university's own official list of past chancellors omits this interim term.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Hathaway had chaired the physics department at Kansas State University for 16 years, then was dean of the College of Sciences and Engineering at the University of Texas at San Antonio (1981-1986) and vice president for academic affairs at Wright State University (1986-1993). As chancellor he returned UALR to an urban/metropolitan mission and created the Cyber College in 1998. He stayed on as a UALR faculty member after 2002 and died August 5, 2025, at age 89.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. A thoroughly internal appointment: Anderson joined UALR in 1971 as an assistant professor of political science, became founding dean of the graduate school in 1977 and provost in 1984, held the provostship for nearly two decades, and was named chancellor in 2003 after an earlier interim term. He served 13 years as chancellor and 45 years at the institution, oversaw the Donaghey College of Engineering, the Jack Stephens Center and three residence halls, and retired effective June 30, 2016; the Anderson Institute on Race and Ethnicity was named for him that year.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Provost
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: interim chancellor. Named interim chancellor on June 28, 2016 upon Joel Anderson's June 30 retirement, she led the campus from July 1 to August 30, 2016, working closely with UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt until Andrew Rogerson began September 1. She was published as Zulma Toro-Ramos when hired as UALR provost in 2012, and in October 2016 was selected as the thirteenth president of Central Connecticut State University, taking office January 3, 2017 as that university's first female and first Hispanic president. She is omitted from the university's official past-chancellors list.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: Sonoma State University (California State University system)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire: UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt selected Rogerson in May 2016 after an eight-month national search that produced three finalists, and he took office September 1, 2016 as the university's tenth chancellor, with an investiture on May 11, 2017. A native of Scotland with a doctorate in protozoan ecology, he had previously held posts at Marshall University and Fresno State. Amid enrollment decline and budget cuts he announced on August 30, 2019 that he would step down effective September 1, 2019, saying it would be best for him to step aside.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Interim Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor; sitting incumbent, so endYear is null. A fully internal appointment: Drale joined UALR in 2006 as associate dean of the College of Professional Studies after nearly 20 years at Missouri State University, became associate vice chancellor for academic affairs in 2011, and was serving as interim executive vice chancellor and provost from October 2018 when UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt named her acting chancellor on September 4-5, 2019 after Andrew Rogerson's forced resignation; the UA Board of Trustees unanimously made the appointment permanent on September 12, 2019. She holds BA, MA and PhD degrees from UC San Diego. She told the UA Board of Trustees in May 2026 (reported May 21-22, 2026) that she will retire effective June 30, 2027, at the end of the 2026-27 academic year, saying "It's just time for me" after about 40 years in higher education, and wanting to finish the university's centennial year and its $250 million Centennial Campaign. UA System President Jay B. Silveria announced the advisory chancellor search committee on July 16, 2026 (reported by the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette on July 23, 2026), chaired by UALR vice provost for research and graduate dean Brian Berry and including UA trustee Ashley Caldwell and Little Rock city director Dean Kumpuris; the committee will work with a search firm and the position is to be advertised beginning early in the fall 2026 semester, with Silveria aiming to identify a successor before Drale departs.

priorInstitution: Little Rock, Arkansas public schools (previously Mattoon, Illinois public schools)
notes: Hired as acting president of the newly opened Arkansas Industrial University because the trustees could not secure a permanent leader; he organized the institution, managed its business affairs, hired faculty and taught courses. The university awarded him an honorary Master of Arts degree in 1880.

priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: A Yale graduate (1853) and former Union Army captain who had been the university's treasurer since its 1871 founding; Old Main opened during his presidency. He left when appointed state adjutant general and ran unsuccessfully for governor in 1875.

priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Second, non-acting term leading the university, returning to the presidency from the normal department after Albert Bishop's departure. He later became superintendent of the Fort Smith school district (1884) and of Fayetteville public schools (1889).

West Point graduate (1842) and Confederate lieutenant general who had chaired mathematics at Washington College and Davidson College before running the North Carolina Military Institute. His administration raised academic standards and grew enrollment; he resigned in 1884 for health reasons.

Virginia-born former Confederate officer whose administration emphasized institutional regulation, holding forty-two faculty meetings before Christmas of his first college year. He resigned in 1887 in opposition to a General Assembly reorganization of the university.

priorTitle: Chair of Mathematics and Logic (then acting president)
priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Promoted from the mathematics and logic chair (1885-1887) to acting president and then confirmed as the university's fifth president. Student attendance rose to roughly 700 during his tenure, which a faculty report called a period of progress unprecedented in the institution's history.

priorTitle: Superintendent of Public Instruction of Virginia (and ex officio member of the University of Virginia board)
notes: A former president of Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, he changed the institution's name from Arkansas Industrial University to University of Arkansas in 1899 and created independent departments of history, civil engineering and electrical engineering. He retired in 1902 for health reasons and returned to Virginia.

A Baptist minister and educator, he was the first University of Arkansas president born after the Civil War and the youngest person to hold the office. He secured funding for several campus buildings still in use, and later entered educational publishing in St. Louis.

priorTitle: President of the alumni association and member of the Board of Trustees (previously prosecuting attorney and circuit judge, 4th Judicial District of Arkansas)
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: A lawyer admitted to the Arkansas bar in 1883, he came to the presidency from the university's own alumni association leadership and board of trustees. He resigned at the end of the 1911-1912 school year and was elected to Congress two years later, serving seven terms.

priorTitle: Chair of History and Political Science
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Acting president who reorganized the teaching departments into three colleges (Agriculture, Arts and Sciences, and Engineering) and created a publicity committee that became the university relations office. Despite campus support, the Board of Trustees passed him over for the permanent post.

priorTitle: Chair of the Mathematics Department (and acting president)
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Longest-serving president in the institution's history; enrollment nearly quadrupled and major campus buildings were constructed during his 26 years. He died in office in a traffic accident near West Fork, Arkansas, on September 12, 1939, while returning from business in Little Rock.

priorInstitution: University of Arkansas School of Law (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Elevated from the law faculty (which he joined in 1936) to the presidency at age 34. His presidency was terminated by trustees newly appointed by Governor Homer Adkins, whom Fulbright's mother Roberta, editor of the Northwest Arkansas Times, had opposed; he went on to the U.S. House in 1942, the Senate in 1944, and a long chairmanship of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

priorTitle: Registrar and Director of General Extension
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: The first Arkansas-born president of the university, promoted after serving as registrar since 1916 and extension director since 1919. He mobilized the campus for World War II, saying the University of Arkansas enlisted for the duration when Pearl Harbor was bombed; he resigned in 1946, served into early 1947, and died in Fayetteville that December.

An economist recruited from Bennington College who oversaw the racial integration of the university, when Silas H. Hunt enrolled in the School of Law, along with creation of the Fine Arts Center and the Medical Center at Little Rock. He left in 1951 for the Rutgers presidency and later led the National Conference of Christians and Jews.

Held a Princeton doctorate and served in the Navy in World War II; at Arkansas he won North Central Association accreditation of doctoral programs, launched the university's first major research push and established a School of Nursing at Fayetteville and the Little Rock Medical Center. He resigned in 1959 for the North Carolina State chancellorship.

priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Acting president named when John Tyler Caldwell resigned, having joined the university in 1954 as an assistant to the president for public relations. When Mullins was appointed president in 1960 he became vice president for health sciences, later leaving in 1970 for the National Institutes of Health.

Came to the presidency after eleven years (1949-1960) as vice president of Auburn University. He retired in 1974; the university's main research library is named in his honor, and he received honorary degrees from Hendrix College (1965) and the University of Arkansas (1987).

An agricultural economist with two decades at North Carolina State before four years as chancellor of the University of Maryland. He built the administrative architecture of what became the University of Arkansas System, creating an executive cabinet and appointing chancellors at the regional campuses, and oversaw construction of Kimpel Hall and a new business building.

priorTitle: Vice President for the Division of Agriculture
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Promoted from within after joining the University of Arkansas in 1975 as vice president for agriculture. As president he created the chancellor's position at the Fayetteville campus, founded the University of Arkansas Press, and built the Center for Continuing Education; he left in 1984 to become president of his alma mater Auburn University, retiring there in 1992.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (a different Arkansas public system, not the UA System)
notes: A former Arkansas attorney general and congressman from the 4th District who came to the UA System presidency directly from three years as president of Arkansas State University in Jonesboro; he moved the president's office to Little Rock. He returned to politics for three more congressional terms, was elected to the Arkansas Supreme Court in 1996 and retired in 2004.

priorTitle: President of Corpus Christi State University (Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi); earlier chancellor of the three-campus South Texas University System
priorInstitution: Corpus Christi State University / Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Texas
notes: A UA-Fayetteville alumnus who returned to his alma mater in 1990 after roughly 22 years in Texas higher education, including about 13 years leading the Corpus Christi institution. Enrollment in the UA System grew from about 30,000 students on five campuses to nearly 70,000 across 17 campuses and units, with roughly $2 billion in construction and renovation.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: A chemist and former dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at UA-Fayetteville (2003) who returned from UT Arlington to begin as system president on November 1, 2011. He founded eVersity, the state's first fully online institution, in 2015, added UA-Pulaski Technical College and UA-Rich Mountain (2016) and East Arkansas Community College (2024), and announced his retirement on July 16, 2024, effective January 15, 2025.

priorTitle: Associate Vice President of Texas A&M University and Executive Director of the Bush School of Government & Public Service in Washington, D.C.
notes: Retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant general and former superintendent of the U.S. Air Force Academy, unanimously approved by the University of Arkansas Board of Trustees on November 18, 2024 and started January 15, 2025. The search that produced him was run for the UA Foundation Board by Greenwood Asher & Associates (Julie Holley and Marion Frenche), with trustee Scott Ford leading; seven candidates formally applied. He remains in office, so the Greenwood Asher engagement is closed and there is no active UA System presidential search.
